t: By the 1780s Saint-Domingue produced about 40 per cent of the sugar and 60 per cent of the coffee consumed in Europe, more than all the British West Indies together, and its taxes were a major source of the French budget.

Between 1681 and 1791 an estimated 790,000 to 860,000 enslaved Africans were brought to its plantations, a third of the whole Atlantic slave trade in 1783–1791; some 5 to 10 per cent died every year, so the population was kept up only by constant importation.

Enslaved Africans and Creoles planned their rising at the Vodou ceremony of Bois Caïman in 1791; slavery was abolished in 1793, Toussaint Louverture's constitution of 1801 declared it abolished for ever, and the French army sent to restore it was beaten at the Battle of Vertières on 18 November 1803.
dyk: Deported to France in 1802, Toussaint Louverture warned his captors: "In overthrowing me you have cut down in Saint-Domingue only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again from the roots, for they are numerous and they are deep."
ev: Louis XIV officially recognises French colonisation of Hispaniola and Tortuga, with slavery-based plantation agriculture and cattle farming.
The Code Noir regulates slavery and grants freed people full citizenship; the colony's first sugar windmill is built.
By the Peace of Ryswick Spain tacitly recognises French control of Tortuga and the western third of Hispaniola.
Mackandal, the one-armed maroon leader who united the maroon bands and raided for six years, is captured after a plot to poison the planters' water and burned alive at Cap-Français.
Some 8,000 plantations worked by 406,000 to 465,000 enslaved people produce half the sugar and coffee consumed in Europe and the Americas.
After the Vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman the enslaved of the northern plain rise, killing 2,000 Creoles and burning 280 sugar plantations within two months.
Civil Commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax abolishes slavery in the colony by emancipation proclamation; Toussaint Louverture joins the Republic.
On 18 November Dessalines's army defeats the French at the Battle of Vertières near Cap-Haïtien; the last French troops withdraw and Haiti declares independence in 1804.

f.capital: Cap-Français (later Cap-Haïtien), established shortly before 1670; Port-au-Prince grew into the economic centre of the south
f.founder: French buccaneers who settled Tortuga in 1625, brought under royal authority by Bertrand d'Ogeron; Louis XIV recognised the colony in 1665
f.predecessor: The western coast of Spanish Hispaniola (La Española, Santo Domingo), depopulated by Governor Antonio de Osorio in 1605
f.successor: Haiti, which declared its independence in 1804 after the last French troops withdrew in late 1803; the Empire of Haiti under Dessalines
